t: Microwaves don't cook from the inside out
b: Microwave ovens make water molecules in food jiggle, which heats it. The waves only penetrate a few centimetres, so the outer layers heat first and the heat spreads inward by conduction. That's why thick food can stay cold in the middle.

q.p: How does a microwave oven heat food?
o: Jiggles water molecules near the surface

rq.p: Why can the middle of thick food stay cold?
o: Microwaves only reach a few cm in

why: Stirring or resting lets heat spread evenly.

b: Most phone screens are capacitive: a grid of tiny electrodes holds an electric field. Your finger conducts electricity and disturbs the field at that spot. Ordinary gloves block this, which is why they don't work on screens.

q.p: Why don't touchscreens work with ordinary gloves?
o: Gloves block your body's electrical effect

rq.p: What do capacitive screens detect?

why: Touchscreen gloves have conductive threads in the fingertips.

b: Noise-cancelling headphones use microphones to listen to the noise around you, then play a sound wave that is its exact mirror image. The peaks of one meet the troughs of the other, and they largely cancel out.

q.p: How do noise-cancelling headphones work?
o: They play an opposite sound wave

rq.p: Which noises are easiest to cancel?

why: Predictable sounds are easy to mirror in time.

b: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks. Because of relativity, their clocks run about 38 microseconds a day faster than clocks on the ground. Without correcting for that, GPS positions would drift by kilometres every day.

q.p: What would happen to GPS without relativity corrections?
o: It would drift by kilometres a day

rq.p: How much faster do GPS satellite clocks run each day?

why: Weaker gravity and high speed both change how fast time passes.
src: Error analysis for the Global Positioning System

b: Your phone doesn't send anything to GPS satellites. It listens for time signals from at least four of them and calculates how far away each one is from how long the signal took. Combining the distances pins down your position.

q.p: Does your phone send signals to GPS satellites?

rq.p: How many satellites does a GPS fix need at minimum?

why: Three give position; the fourth corrects your phone's clock.

b: A fridge doesn't make cold; it moves heat. A refrigerant liquid evaporates inside, soaking up heat, then a compressor squeezes it so it releases that heat through coils at the back. That's why the back of a fridge feels warm.

q.p: Why is the back of a fridge warm?
o: It dumps heat taken from inside

rq.p: What soaks up heat inside a fridge?

why: Evaporation absorbs heat, the same way sweat cools you.

t: The 'equal time' wing explanation is wrong
b: A common explanation says air over a wing's curved top must reach the back at the same time as air below, so it speeds up. It doesn't: top air actually arrives first. Wings make lift by turning air downward, creating lower pressure above.

q.p: Does air over a wing reach the back at the same time as air below?

rq.p: How do wings really make lift?

why: Pushing air down pushes the wing up.

b: Sunlight contains every colour. As it passes through air, tiny gas molecules scatter short blue wavelengths much more than red ones. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all over the sky.

q.p: Why is the sky blue?

rq.p: Why are sunsets red?
o: Light passes through more air, scattering away blue

why: This is called Rayleigh scattering.

t: Card chips make a one-time code
b: When you pay with a chip card, the chip generates a unique code for that one transaction using a secret key that never leaves the card. A copied code is useless for another payment, which is why chips cut card cloning.

q.p: What does your bank card chip create for each payment?
o: Nothing, it just stores your number

rq.p: Why can't criminals reuse a copied chip code?

why: Magnetic stripes repeated the same data, so they were easy to clone.

b: Contactless payment uses near-field communication (NFC). The reader's magnetic field powers the card's chip and exchanges data, but only over very short distances, typically up to about 4 cm.

q.p: How close must a contactless card usually be?

rq.p: What powers a contactless card's chip?

why: The short range is a deliberate security feature.

b: QR codes contain built-in error correction. At the highest setting, up to about 30% of a code can be dirty, torn or covered by a logo and it will still scan correctly.

q.p: How much of a QR code can be damaged and still scan?

rq.p: Why can logos sit in the middle of QR codes?
o: Error correction fills in missing parts

why: Extra redundant data lets the scanner rebuild missing bits.

b: The last digit of a standard product barcode is a check digit, worked out by a simple sum of the other digits. If the scanner misreads a number, the sum won't match and it rejects the scan instead of charging for the wrong item.

q.p: What is the last digit of a product barcode for?

rq.p: What happens if a barcode check doesn't match?

why: A cheap calculation catches most misreads.

t: Wi-Fi and microwaves share a frequency
b: Many Wi-Fi networks use the 2.4 GHz radio band, the same region microwave ovens use to heat food. Ovens are shielded, but a little leakage can slow Wi-Fi while someone heats lunch.

q.p: Which kitchen appliance can interfere with Wi-Fi?

rq.p: Which frequency band do they share?

why: The 2.4 GHz band is open for anyone to use without a licence.

t: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king
b: Bluetooth is named after Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson, a 10th-century king who united Danish tribes. The tech was meant to unite devices. Its logo combines the runes for his initials, H and B.

q.p: Who is Bluetooth named after?

rq.p: What does the Bluetooth logo show?

why: Uniting tribes became a metaphor for uniting gadgets.

t: The @ in email was a quick choice
b: In 1971, engineer Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email between two computers. He picked @ to separate the user from the computer's name because it was on the keyboard and didn't appear in names.

q.p: Why did Ray Tomlinson choose @ for email?

rq.p: When was the first networked email sent?

why: 'user at computer' read naturally.

b: Each extra character multiplies the guesses an attacker needs. A long passphrase of several random words is usually harder to crack than a short jumble like 'P@55w0rd!', and easier to remember. Modern security guidance favours length.

q.p: Which is usually stronger?

rq.p: Why does length matter so much?

why: Attackers guess common substitutions like @ for a.

t: The padlock doesn't mean a site is safe
b: The padlock in your browser means your connection is encrypted, so others can't read the data in transit. It doesn't prove the website is honest; scam sites can have padlocks too.

q.p: What does the browser padlock mean?

rq.p: Can scam sites show a padlock?

why: Encryption certificates are free and easy to get.

t: Incognito mode hides less than you think
b: Private browsing stops your browser saving history and cookies on your device. Websites, your employer or school network, and your internet provider can still see what you visit.

q.p: Who can still see your visits in incognito mode?

rq.p: What does incognito mode actually stop?

why: It's privacy from others using your device, not from the internet.

b: Lithium-ion batteries wear out faster when hot or kept at full charge for long periods. That's why many phones now pause charging around 80% overnight. Leaving a phone in a hot car is one of the worst things for its battery.

q.p: What wears out phone batteries fastest?

rq.p: Why do phones pause charging around 80% overnight?

why: Heat and high charge speed up chemical side-reactions.

b: To estimate how long it takes money to double with compound interest, divide 72 by the yearly interest rate. At 6% a year, money doubles in about 12 years. At 9%, about 8 years.

q.p: Roughly how long does money take to double at 6% a year?

rq.p: What's the Rule of 72 used for?

why: Compound growth earns interest on past interest.

t: Banks create most money by lending
b: Most money in a modern economy isn't notes and coins but bank deposits. The Bank of England explains that when a bank makes a loan, it creates a new deposit in the borrower's account, effectively creating new money.

q.p: Where does most money in the UK come from?

rq.p: What happens when a bank makes a loan?

why: The Bank of England described this in a 2014 paper.

t: The Bank of England targets 2% inflation
b: The Bank of England's target is to keep inflation around 2% a year. It mainly does this by changing interest rates: raising them makes borrowing pricier and cools spending, while lowering them encourages spending.

q.p: What inflation rate does the Bank of England aim for?

rq.p: What's the Bank's main tool for controlling inflation?

why: A little inflation is thought healthier than falling prices.

t: The first number sways your guess
b: In a famous 1974 study, people saw a wheel of fortune land on a number before estimating how many African countries were in the UN. Those who saw a higher number gave higher guesses. This is the anchoring effect.

q.p: What did a random wheel number change in the anchoring study?

rq.p: Who described the anchoring effect?

why: We adjust from a starting point, but not far enough.

t: Losses hurt more than gains feel good
b: Research on loss aversion suggests losing something feels roughly twice as bad as gaining the same thing feels good. It explains why people hold onto falling shares and hate giving up things they own.

q.p: Losing £10 typically feels…

rq.p: What's this tendency called?

why: Avoiding losses may have helped our ancestors survive.

b: In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables and tested himself. He found memory drops steeply within the first day, then levels off. Reviewing at spaced intervals flattens the curve, the idea Inkling's reviews are built on.

q.p: When do we forget new things fastest?

rq.p: What flattens the forgetting curve?

why: Each well-timed review makes the memory more durable.
